title: Sex life: I don’t police my clients’ morals
gist: Sydney sex worker Tilly Lawless, with 13 years and 3,000-6,000 clients, explains why she judges clients only on in-room conduct, not their morals, politics or income source. She argues the transactional relationship reveals only a curated slice of a person, and that moral screening would be financially unsustainable.

insights.claim: A veteran Australian sex worker reports seeing between 3,000 and 6,000 clients over 13 years of work.
insights.so_what: Gives a sense of scale and client throughput in independent full-service sex work.
insights.quote: I have seen over 3,000, and perhaps as many as 6,000, clients in my 13 years of sex work.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless

insights.claim: Lawless screens clients solely on respect for her, her time and her boundaries, not on income source or value alignment, arguing that being paid is not an endorsement of the client.
insights.so_what: Illustrates a 'conduct-not-character' screening norm that contrasts with growing values-based gatekeeping in other service sectors.
insights.quote: being paid to see them is no public, or even, private endorsement of them
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless

insights.claim: Lawless argues that morally vetting clients' outside lives would make sex work financially unsustainable for her, though some peers refuse clients connected to any military.
insights.so_what: Shows the economic cost of ethical screening for sole-trader service workers.
insights.quote: if I made it my business it wouldn’t be financially sustainable for me to be in this business
insights.locator: A friend of mine doesn’t see
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless

insights.claim: Because the relationship is transactional, a sex worker only sees the side a client chooses to present in the room; one gentle regular sent abusive messages via Instagram.
insights.so_what: Highlights how social media exposes service workers to client behaviour outside controlled settings.
insights.quote: our relationship is forever transactional—we only see the sides we choose to show to each other in that moment
insights.locator: I used to have a regular
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless

insights.claim: Lawless avoids political arguments with clients partly for physical safety, since escalating conflict alone in a room with a larger man is dangerous.
insights.so_what: Safety constraints shape how workers in isolated service roles handle polarised clients.
insights.quote: it’s never a good idea to incite or escalate conflict when you are alone in a room with a man who is much bigger than you
insights.locator: I don’t argue politics with clients
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless

insights.claim: During Australia's gay marriage plebiscite, Lawless says many clients went on homophobic rants, which she tactfully appeased rather than confronted.
insights.so_what: Anecdotal window into private male attitudes during a major Australian social referendum.
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless

insights.claim: Lawless finds that reframing objections to a right-wing politician in terms of secularism rather than racism persuaded a One Nation-voting, Peter Dutton-loving client in a way direct criticism would not.
insights.so_what: Suggests persuasion of right-leaning voters works better via shared-value framing than accusations of racism.
insights.quote: he absorbs that response in a way he wouldn’t the other and says I’ve made him look at it in a way he hasn’t before
insights.speaker: Tilly Lawless
